title: The numinous
hookLine: Rudolf Otto named the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and draws us in (The Idea of the Holy)
last: THE COSMOS HAS A WAY TO KNOW ITSELF.

lines: A NEW WORD FOR THE HOLY.
cards: A storm rolls in after dark. The power cuts out. Lightning shows the whole street for half a second, then nothing.
Some people pull the curtains shut. Others drift to the window, a little scared, and can't stop looking. Back away, come closer, both at once.

Rudolf Otto, a scholar of religion, wrote a whole book about that double pull. He thought it sat near the heart of what people mean by holy, and that the old words weren't good enough for it. He needed a new one.

teach.b: The book is The Idea of the Holy. First, his complaint. When people say holy, Otto noticed, they often just mean perfectly good.
That leaves something out: something stranger than goodness, a sense of a presence that is wholly other. So from the Latin numen, a word for divine power or presence, he formed numinous.
Second, he said the numinous can't be strictly defined, only pointed at until the listener recognizes it, the way you'd help someone recognize a smell.
So he gave it a Latin description: mysterium tremendum et fascinans. Mysterium: a mystery, beyond our grasp. Tremendum: something to tremble before, so overwhelming it makes a person feel small.
He called that creature-feeling. Third, the half that's easy to miss: fascinans. For Otto the holy doesn't only frighten.
It attracts, and the trembling and the drawing near arrive together. Fourth, an old scene that holds both halves.
In Exodus, Moses sees a bush burning that doesn't burn up, and in the King James words he says, "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight." He walks toward it.
A moment later, "Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God." Toward, and away.
Otto was a Christian theologian, and readers argue about his theology. His word has traveled far beyond his book.
A storm, a birth, the sea at night, a silence in a very old room: some moments ask for a bigger word than nice. Numinous is one.

how: Students of religion use Rudolf Otto's word numinous for the sense of a holy presence that is both overwhelming and attractive; some people who practice no religion use it for moments in nature or music that feel too large for ordinary words.

games.q: you're Moses. a bush is burning in the desert and it isn't burning up. what do you do?
o: turn aside to see it, then hide your face.
call others to come and watch.
games.why: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight" — and then "Moses hid his face; for he was afraid." toward and away: Otto's double pull in one scene.

practice: Bring back one moment that made you tremble, not from danger alone but from something too big: a storm, a newborn, the ocean after dark, a silence in an old building.
Stand in it again, notice whether part of you wanted to step back and part wanted to step closer, and let both be there without explaining the moment. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Numinous. Rudolf Otto's word for the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and draws us in. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: divine power or presence. Otto formed the word numinous from it.

carryVoice: Your line: tremble and draw near. The holy, in Otto's telling, does both at once. Same time tomorrow.
